title: Educational Reform for Equitable EFL TPACK Development: Contextual Barriers and Opportunities in Iranian Public Schools and Private Institutes
abstract: Current education reforms couple technology integration with the pursuit of equity transforming how teachers learn and teach. This study explored the role of institutional context in Iranian EFL teachers’ development of technological pedagogical and content knowledge (TPACK). Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the data were collected from 94 teachers through convenience sampling. A TPACK self-assessment survey and purposive semistructured interviews provided quantitative and qualitative insights. Results from SPSS 21 showed that private institute teachers significantly outperformed their public school counterparts across all TPACK domains, especially in technological knowledge and technological pedagogical knowledge. NVivo 12 analysis revealed that outdated infrastructure, rigid curricula, and limited professional development hindered public school teachers, while private institutes offered stronger support and technological access. Conceptualizing TPACK as a context-dependent construct, the study recognizes the urgency of reforms for facilitating greater digital access, designing flexible curricula, and ensuring regular professional development for equitable and

title: Preparation and Practice: Examining Pre-Service Teachers’ Negotiated Experiences Facilitating Students’ Knowledge and Academic Development
abstract: There remains an urgent call for teacher educators to prepare prospective teachers in ways that lead to the use of equity pedagogies in mathematics classrooms. This investigation used a qualitative methodology to analyze interviews with pre-service secondary mathematics teachers using Hernandez, Shroyer, and Morales's framework for culturally responsive mathematics teaching. Findings point to a need for explicit theory-to-practice research about utilizing cultural relevancy in mathematics teaching and learning. Implications exist for how teacher educators can use professional modeling to disrupt the disconnection between how teachers are prepared and what they eventually do at their practice sites.

title: Positive and Negative Affect in Curriculum Reform: Insights From Teachers in Kosovo
abstract: This study explores how teachers’ emotions affect curriculum reform implementation in Kosovo. Using data from 163 teachers and guided by emotional labor theory, it examines the effects of positive and negative affect on understanding, applying, and perceiving a new competency-based curriculum. Results show that positive affect significantly enhances teachers’ comprehension, use of student-centered methods, and practical application, while negative affect is linked to lower understanding and more negative perceptions of reform. These findings underscore the crucial role of emotions in shaping educational change and highlight the need for emotional support to ensure successful and sustainable curriculum implementation.

title: Beyond Synchronisation: Developing the Pedagogy of Rhythmic Embodiment for Post-Standardisation Education
abstract: Educational responses to temporal difference often adjust pacing or scheduling while leaving learning organisation unchanged. This exploratory study asks what pedagogical form becomes possible when temporal plurality is treated as constitutive of learning. Drawing on multi-source fieldwork in Vietnam and vernacular pedagogical units, it identifies four recurrent functions – Reception, Integration, Restoration and Expression – that overlap, recur and vary in duration. From these relations, the study proposes the Pedagogy of Rhythmic Embodiment as a provisional architecture of coordination through transition, offering initial support and a testable agenda without claiming efficacy or universal transferability.

title: Global Competitiveness and Educational Change: Perspectives About English as the Medium of Instruction in Kazakhstan's Universities
abstract: To become globally competitive, Kazakhstan has been introducing higher education benchmarks and quality scholastic services to match those in advanced countries. The administration's policy for higher education reform is a degree of convergence, that is, catching up with the developed knowledge-based economies of North America and Europe, enabling entry into the European Union (EU) and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). To enhance global competitiveness, the government set out to implement policies promoting English as a medium of instruction (EMI) in universities. Therefore, a crucial area of higher education reform in Kazakhstan has been promoting English to develop human capital and modernize education in line with international standards, thereby training scientific and teaching staff. In addition, higher education reform has aimed at integrating Kazakhstan into the global research and education space. This article is a case study of language reforms in two major universities in Kazakhstan that have adopted English as the medium of instruction. The purpose of this study is to investigate the implications of adopting English as the medium of instru

title: Private Higher Education Institutions’ Dilemma on National Exit Exam: Challenges, Opportunities, and the Way Forward
abstract: Aims to identify key challenges and propose strategies for balancing quality assurance with institutional autonomy. From 170 initial sources, 53 were included in the final analysis. Data were extracted using a structured charting tool and synthesized thematically. The review identified four major challenges faced by Ethiopian private higher education institutions (PHEIs) in implementing national exit exams: misalignment with standardized curricula, limited resources, lack of information and training, and political social biases. Despite these barriers, national exams also offer opportunities for academic improvement, international recognition, and greater policy influence. PHEIs can leverage these exams to raise standards, enhance credibility, and engage in collaborative reforms.

title: Assessing Teaching Funding Schemes in Taiwan's Higher Education: Insights from University Project Coordinators
abstract: Since the 1990s, competitive funding schemes have become increasingly prevalent in East Asia, requiring universities to compete for resources tied to performance indicators. While research has examined scheme design and implementation, evidence is drawn primarily from research funding, leaving teaching funding underexplored. Drawing on resource dependence theory, this study investigated two Taiwanese schemes: the Program for Promoting Teaching Excellence and the Higher Education Sprout Project. Using interviews with project coordinators and qualitative content analysis, three institutional responses were identified: leveraging resources for institutional advancement, strategic adaptation to funding requirements, and navigating constraints in institutional implementation. Findings highlight tensions between accountability, autonomy, and educational improvement.

title: Evaluating Student Satisfaction in Undergraduate Biology Programs: A Case Study of Injibara University
abstract: This study evaluates undergraduate satisfaction with Injibara University's Biology program, addressing a gap in measuring nine academic quality dimensions. Guided by Astin's Input–Environment–Outcome model and Tinto's student integration, a survey of 53 students revealed an overall satisfaction rate of 84.6%, with high scores for teaching–learning (88.1%), program outcomes (92.4%), and continuous improvement (88.7%). Lower satisfaction emerged for research engagement (69.8%), resources (81.1%), and support services (83.0%), especially counseling and information and communication technology. One-way ANOVA showed significant cohort differences for program outcomes [ F (2,50) = 4.82, p = .012], research [ F (2,50) = 6.14, p = .004], and resources [ F (2,50) = 3.89, p = .027]. Recommendations include targeted resource allocation, enhanced support services, early experiential learning, and inclusive governance to strengthen academic quality and student experience.

title: School Dropout Among Secondary Students: A Study of Two Indian States
abstract: In India, secondary education serves a critical stage for higher education and the workforce. However, it faces alarmingly high dropout rates. Despite widespread prevalence, its causes and effective intervention strategies remain unaddressed. Drawing on a sample of 154 government secondary schools, using mixed methods, chi-square test and binary logistic regression analysis, the article examines indicators and factors contributing to student dropout at the secondary level in two Indian states: Odisha and Assam. Findings of the study reveal that school distance, inadequate sports facilities, migration, child labour, and limited parental and community support significantly influence dropout in varying degrees, emphasising the need for targeted, context-specific interventions.

title: Job Satisfaction of Early Career Teachers of English: The Role in Teacher Retention and Attrition in the Bangladeshi Higher Education Context
abstract: This article employed a mixed-methods research design to determine how job satisfaction affects the future trajectory of early career teachers (ECTs), leading to either retention or career switch in the Bangladeshi EFL context. Close-ended questionnaire survey ( n = 100) was used to collect quantitative data. Besides, interviews ( n = 20) and focus group discussions ( n = 6) were taken of the ECTs working in different universities to collect data on the role of job satisfaction in determining their retention of teaching as a profession or teacher attrition of leaving the profession. Analysis of the responses of the ECTs to the questionnaire via thematic analysis revealed three major challenges: (a) salary and fringe benefits, (b) job security, and (c) teacher autonomy and working conditions. The impact of job satisfaction on teacher attrition or retention includes (a) teacher autonomy and salary having strong to moderate retention rates (b) working conditions having a neutral impact, and (c) teacher autonomy having a moderate impact on teacher attrition or retention among ECTs. The discussion of this article demonstrated the dual role of salary and fringe benefits leading to both t

title: The Synergy of Local Wisdom and Ecoliteracy: A Novel Approach to Instrument Development in Indonesian Education
abstract: Ecoliteracy is an educational approach that integrates ecological and sustainability principles into learning, focusing on the relationship between humans and the environment. This approach links environmental education with local wisdom and traditional knowledge to provide a holistic view. This research aims to develop an ecoliteracy instrument based on local wisdom for university students. The instrument development process includes three stages: (1) development of dimensions, items, and expert validation; (2) exploratory factor analysis (EFA), content validity test, and data reduction; and (3) internal consistency test through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). The results identified seven dimensions of ecoliteracy with a total of 30 items: (1) spiritual values and sacredness of nature (seven items), (2) traditional sustainability practices (six items), (3) togetherness and community (five items), (4) folklore and local knowledge (five items), (5) dimensions of environmental ethics (three items), and (6) contextual adaptation (two items). The instrument was proven valid and reliable through EFA and CFA tests. Ecoliteracy assessment based on local wisdom uses multiple-choice tes

title: Connecting Children to Science: A Qualitative Content Analysis of Science Textbook
abstract: Since experiential learning promotes meaningful understanding through experience and interaction with the environment, it is important that early science textbooks support such approaches. This study aimed at exploring the pertinence of first-grade science textbooks to concrete experiences, reflective observations, abstract conceptualizations, and active experimentations. A directed qualitative content analysis was conducted using Kolb's experiential learning model and Vygotsky's constructivist theory as analytical frameworks. The qualitative content analysis revealed that while reflective observational learning and abstract conceptualization phases are well represented, concrete experiences are only fairly represented and active experimentation opportunities are found rare across all units. The findings dictated that the balanced pertinence of the four stages of learning in the experiential learning model is the major missing component of the textbook. It can be safely concluded that first-grade children are almost connected to environmental sciences, except that the textbook left children with rare opportunities for active experimentation. title: Transforming University Students’ Perspectives and Behaviours in Education for Sustainable Development: Evidence From an Emerging Nation-Malaysia
abstract: Emerging nations’ education systems are reforming their approaches to education for sustainable development (ESD). However, searching for an effective approach continues. This study examines the outcomes of a university's purpose-led, impact-driven learning in Malaysia, aligning with UNESCO's values-led, whole-institution, and action-oriented learning. Guided by Transformative Learning Theory, surveys collected data from module leaders and students across disciplines over two semesters. The findings showed the positive effect on students’ perspectives towards the world and themselves, while the impact on students’ behaviour is comparatively low. This study offers an emerging ESD model that supports the sustainability education reform agenda of emerging countries.

title: Generation Z and Quality Standards in Management Education: Developing a Tri-Dimensional Scale for Excellence
abstract: The quest for quality in management education requires urgent attention with the emergence of Generation Z workforce. The literature falls short of providing a comprehensive scale for quality management education. The authors adopted a mixed-method approach for conducting the study. Fifteen qualitative interviews with faculty, students, and industry professionals were conducted, and helped to craft 49 questions in final questionnaire. Eight factors extracted using principal component analysis, subsequently these factors were clubbed into three dimensions. This novel study promises to expand our understanding by offering multiple implications for addressing SDG goals and providing valuable insights for future research and policymaking.

title: “Behind the Scores”: A Qualitative Exploration of Mock Exam Experiences Among University Entrance Candidates
abstract: This qualitative study seeks to address how high school students preparing for the university entrance examination navigate their experiences during mock exams. The participants were 50 high school students. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis, which yielded six major themes: the subject that started at the beginning of the exam session, responses to challenging questions, environmental and internal distractions during the exam, emotional reactions when torn between two options, coping strategies under time pressure, and procedures related to optical form completion. Themes offered deeper insight into students’ stress responses, time management struggles, and decision-making processes during test-taking.

title: Gender Integration, Workplace Incivility, and Career Advancement in a Public Higher Education Institution in the Philippines
abstract: This study examines the relationships between gender integration, workplace incivility, and perceived career advancement in a public higher education institution. A cross-sectional online survey of 190 participants used validated instruments, including the Gender Mainstreaming Evaluation Framework, the Workplace Incivility Scale, and career advancement measures. Results show high levels of gender integration and low levels of workplace incivility. Non-teaching and administrative staff report higher levels of incivility than teaching personnel. Gender integration is positively associated with career advancement. Instigated incivility is also positively associated with salary and career advancement. The findings highlight the need for gender-inclusive environments to reduce incivility and improve employee outcomes.

title: Non-Formal Vocational Education and its Influence on Human Capital Development in Uganda
abstract: This study investigated the relationship between youth in Northern Uganda's human capital development (HCD) and non-formal vocational education (NFVE). Data were obtained from 60 youths at four NFVE centers in Lira City using a mixed-methods technique. There was no discernible gender difference in productive ability, according to an independent t-test (t(58) = 1.04, p = .46). NFVE involvement and HCD were strongly positively correlated (r = 0.76, p

title: Catalyzed Collaborative Governance: A Conceptual Framework for Addressing the Special Education Teacher Shortages in Indonesia
abstract: The shortage of special education teachers (SETs) is a global challenge that threatens the realization of the right to equitable education for students with special educational needs. In developing countries, this issue reflects multidimensional challenges in public governance. Using a qualitative approach grounded in constructivist grounded theory, this study examines how key actors construct meaning around SET shortages, interact across institutional boundaries, and build the initial foundations for collaborative governance. Data analysis yielded a conceptual framework, Catalyzed Collaborative Governance, that highlights the role of catalytic processes in fostering cross-sector collaboration in contexts where shared agendas and inter-institutional reflective capacities have not yet fully developed.

title: An Exploratory Investigation of ELT Instructors’ Attitudes Toward Bilingual Medium of Instruction (BMI) and the Role of Technology in Bangladeshi Classrooms
abstract: This study investigates the outlooks, reported practices, and perceived constraints of English Language Teaching (ELT) instructors concerning Bilingual Medium of Instruction (BMI) in Bangladeshi university classrooms. Eighteen instructors from Feni University participated in a structured survey. The research is organized around three objectives: (a) examining instructors’ perceptions of translanguaging practices, (b) investigating the obstacles they report when implementing bilingual instruction, and (c) exploring how technological integration may facilitate translanguaging pedagogy. Within this sample, 88.9% of respondents indicated support for bilingual instruction, citing enhanced comprehension, increased learner confidence, and faster learning as the most frequently reported benefits. Approximately 66.7% of participants expressed concern about reduced English exposure, and a majority reported inadequate training, restrictive institutional policies, and limited bilingual resources as recurring barriers. Respondents held positive attitudes toward AI-driven tools and gamification, although the extent of implementation appeared to vary with available resources. The study discusses

title: Teacher Professional Identity as the Human Infrastructure of Multi-Tiered Systems of Support in Secondary Schools
abstract: The Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) framework is widely adopted at the secondary level, yet implementation often remains difficult to sustain due to logistical constraints, inconsistent application, and limited teacher engagement. As adolescent literacy needs continue to intensify, effective intervention becomes increasingly important, yet much of the existing research has emphasized systemic barriers rather than the cognitive and professional factors that shape teacher-driven implementation. This study addresses that gap by examining Teacher Professional Identity (TPI) as a meaningful but underexplored factor associated with MTSS implementation, with specific attention to how teachers’ perceptions of autonomy, competence, and professional relationships relate to their self-reported implementation practices. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, quantitative data from 85 secondary educators established statistical relationships between TPI and MTSS implementation, while 12 semi-structured interviews provided qualitative depth into teachers’ lived experiences. Findings revealed that higher levels of TPI were correlated with stronger perceived MTSS implementati

title: Parenting Style and Academic Procrastination: A Serial Mediation Role of Social Media Usage and Fear of Failure
abstract: This study examined the relationship between parenting styles and academic procrastination (AP), with social media usage (SMU) and fear of failure (FoF) as serial mediators. Data from 327 participants aged 18–22 were analyzed using SPSS 27 and PROCESS Macro Model 6. Authoritative parenting negatively predicted AP, whereas authoritarian and permissive parenting positively predicted AP. Significant indirect effects emerged for authoritative and authoritarian parenting through SMU and FoF, while permissive parenting showed no significant mediation effect. Findings highlight the importance of behavioral and emotional mechanisms in understanding and reducing AP.

title: Visualizing Trends in Chat Generative Pretrained Transformer Research in Higher Education: Early-Stage Bibliometric Analysis
abstract: The rapid emergence of chat generative pretrained transformer (ChatGPT) has attracted considerable attention in higher education (HE), yet its research development remains insufficiently understood. This study provides an early-stage bibliometric analysis of 140 Scopus-indexed articles to map research trends in this field. The results show a sharp increase in publications, with China, the United States, and the United Kingdom as the leading contributors. Co-occurrence analysis identified three major themes: educational applications, learner interactions, and technological dimensions. Overlay visualization revealed emerging topics such as intention, relationship, and social influence, indicating a growing focus on adoption and behavioral aspects of ChatGPT in HE.

title: Comparative Analysis of Sports Participation in Tanzanian Secondary Schools: Implications for Reform
abstract: The need to identify disparities and opportunities in sports participation across Tanzanian secondary schools is vital for informing policies for sports development. This study, therefore, offers an understanding of the comparative analysis of sports participation in secondary schools. Through a mixed-methods research approach, triangulated data from surveys and interviews involving 427 participants revealed high participation in ball games such as football, netball, basketball, and volleyball, whereas sports such as tennis, badminton, swimming, and aerobics recorded minimal participation. Limited facilities constrained participation in certain sports, though schools made efforts to encourage students’ involvement through structuring sports programmes and extracurricular activities as well as improvising resources when necessary. The findings imply that it is imperative to reform sports programmes to cater for the diverse needs of all students and promote their participation. Also, schools need to reform the structure of accessing resources and strengthen policy enforcement to prioritize the running of sports activities. This study concludes that to enhance participation, schools s

title: Reforming CPD Practices for English Language Teachers in Namibia: The Role of Self-Directed Professional Learning
abstract: This study explored the potential of self-directed learning (SDL) to reform continuous professional development (CPD) for English second language (ESL) teachers in Namibia, where centralized, top-down CPD models have failed to address classroom realities. Through a qualitative case study of secondary school ESL teachers in the Khomas region, the research identifies systemic gaps in Namibia's CPD framework, including inadequate teacher agency, lack of specialized training, and resource constraints. Findings reveal that SDL empowers teachers to address context-specific challenges through collaborative peer networks, reflective practice, and grassroots initiatives, aligning with social constructivist theories and reflective practice frameworks. However, institutional barriers and under-resourcing hinder sustainable implementation. The study advocates for decentralized, teacher-led CPD models that prioritize autonomy, collaboration, and contextual relevance, offering a pathway to improve ESL instruction and align with global best practices in teacher professional development.

title: Optional Courses to Enhance Employability in Higher Education: An Experience of the Curriculum Change in a Centralized Education System
abstract: The study aims to reflect the lived experiences of professors and curriculum specialists about the functions and challenges of optional courses in the higher education curriculum. The impetus behind this study was to enhance the employability of undergraduate students. To fulfill this purpose, the qualitative research method was used to gather the data on participants’ lived experiences. For this purpose, the participants were selected through the purposeful snowball sampling method. The data were collected through individual interviews. The themes related to the function of implementing optional courses in the curriculum included enhancing technical and core competencies, facilitating employment, enriching the curriculum, interdisciplinary functions, the emergence of multiple identities in students, and attention to social needs. The results of the research on the challenges of incorporating optional courses into the higher education curriculum fell into two major categories: development challenges and implementation challenges including: resistance to curriculum changes, an imbalance between main and optional courses, misperception of optional courses, expanding the curriculum an

title: Let's Talk Money: Assessing the Need of Incorporating Financial Education in Dental Curriculum—A Logistic Regression Analysis
abstract: Introduction Financial literacy is essential for managing debt, planning for retirement, and making informed money-related decisions. However, in India—especially in healthcare education—this important skill is often overlooked. For dental professionals, understanding their current financial knowledge, mindset, and habits is the first step toward addressing this gap. This study set out to assess the financial literacy of dental practitioners in Maharashtra and emphasize its importance in the current economic context. Materials and Methods A cross-sectional survey was carried out among 460 registered dental practitioners across five regions of Maharashtra, using a stratified sampling method. Participants completed a validated, self-administered questionnaire over a two-month period, which collected demographic details and evaluated financial awareness, attitude, and behavior. Data analysis included descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests for group comparisons, Spearman's correlation for relationships among financial domains, and logistic regression to examine links between participant characteristics and financial literacy. A p -value of less than .05 indicated statistical signific

title: How Science Teachers Foster Critical Thinking in Junior Secondary Classrooms: A Narrative Inquiry from a Constructivist Perspective
abstract: The narrative inquiry explored junior high school science teachers' reported practices in fostering students' critical thinking skills in Indonesia using a narrative inquiry approach guided by a critical thinking framework. Data were collected from October to November 2024 through semi-structured interviews and classroom observations involving science teachers at the junior high school level. The findings indicate that teachers frequently implemented student-centered instructional approaches, including problem-based learning, project-based learning, inquiry learning, and discovery learning, to encourage interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, and self-regulation. Teachers also emphasized contextual problems, collaborative discussions, scaffolding, reflective questioning, and evidence-based reasoning to support students' thinking processes. Classroom observations confirmed the presence of instructional practices intended to encourage active participation, argumentation, reflection, and analytical reasoning. However, the findings represent teachers' reported practices and observed classroom interactions rather than direct evidence of students' critical thinking

title: Defensive School Choice: Parents Escaping Unequal Schooling in India
abstract: The growing preference for private schooling in India has intensified concerns regarding educational inequality and declining trust in public education. Drawing on Pierre Bourdieu's concept of cultural capital, this qualitative study explored why parents prefer private schooling despite free education. Interviews with ten parents across India revealed that parental preference was shaped by concerns regarding educational quality, disparity, unequal opportunities, and preparedness within public schooling systems. Parents’ choice was linked with anxieties regarding children's mobility and competitiveness. The study proposes the notion of “defensive school choice,” suggesting that parental migration toward private schooling reflected educational insecurity rather than unrestricted preference.

title: “We are not Ineffective Educators”: Forced Solidarity and Teacher Resistance in Kazakhstan's Targeted Schools
abstract: This study examines how teachers in Kazakhstan experience the implementation of a large-scale, top-down school improvement initiative, the “Targeted Schools” program. Drawing on semistructured interviews with 32 teachers across three regions, thematic analysis revealed three patterns: administrative shock stemming from opaque school selection criteria; superficial professional development characterized by misaligned content and compulsory testing under degrading conditions; and psycho-emotional burnout accompanied by defensive collective behavior, the study conceptualizes as forced solidarity. The findings demonstrate how uncritical policy borrowing produces compliance without genuine improvement, and how accountability-driven reform, absent adequate capacity and relational trust, systematically undermines teacher professional identity. Implications for the design of equitable school improvement policy are discussed.

title: Book Review: The Teacher Wars: A History of America’s Most Embattled Profession by Goldstein, Dana The Teacher Wars: A History of America’s Most Embattled Profession. GoldsteinDana. New York: Doubleday, 2014. 349 pp. $26.95 (hardcopy).
Psychometric Validation of an Early Childhood Social-Emotional Development Assessment Instrument: Evidence for Fair and Reliable Educational Evaluation
abstract: This study aimed to validate an instrument for assessing early childhood social-emotional development using a comprehensive psychometric approach. The instrument was tested through exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), the generalized partial credit model (GPCM), and differential item functioning (DIF). The results showed strong construct validity, high internal consistency, and good item discrimination with appropriate difficulty levels. DIF analysis indicated no significant gender bias, confirming measurement fairness across boys and girls. The validated instrument provides teachers with a systematic and evidence-based tool for identifying developmental needs, planning interventions, and improving classroom-based assessment practices in early childhood education.

title: Job Competencies of School Principals During the Next 10 Years (2023–2032): A Case Study of Bangkok Metropolitan Administration Schools
abstract: Education is one of the critical factors influencing a nation's future development. This notion is recognized internationally and clearly shown in the United Nation's 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. Competent school principals are an important factor in the achievement of educational goals and quality educational outcomes. This research, therefore, studies the competencies expected of school principals in Bangkok Metropolitan Administration Schools (BMAS) over the next 10 years (2023–2032). The Ethnographic Delphi Futures Research (Ethnographic Futures Research plus Delphi technique) and Delphi techniques were employed to analyze data obtained from interviews of 50 selected BMA executives, human resource managers, and school principals who are knowledgeable about the work of BMAS. The findings indicate that the following competencies are crucial for school principals in the future: intrapreneurial aptitude, multilingual proficiency, organizational engagement, administrative skills, creativity, and technological fluency. It is recommended that, based on the research findings, ethical leadership should also be explicitly stated as one of the competencies for principals.

title: Our Universities, Their Priorities? A Case for Afrocentric Ranking of Universities in East Africa
abstract: Are university rankings neocolonial structures pressurizing universities in East Africa to pursue priorities that are irrelevant to their deserving social service mandate? Referencing relevant trends and literature, we demonstrate that available evidence discredits the widely held view that this is the case. That although perceptions of victimhood encourage skepticism against them, rankings are neither against universities here nor without benefits. That despite their unarguable shortfalls, rankings have enormous power and are directing the development of university education worldwide. Universities here cannot wish this power away. However, the universities could ensure that they are validly ranked, to leverage the power of rankings to advance their missions. However, they have not done this because they suffer from various weaknesses. We argue that these weaknesses, rather than rankings that mirror them, are the problem. Therefore, we urge attention to the weaknesses and development of Afrocentric rankings.

title: Evaluating Public-Private Partnerships in Education: Evidence from Government-Subsidized Low-Cost Private Schools in Sindh, Pakistan
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the impact of the government subsidies on low-cost private schools in Sindh, Pakistan, under the Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) policy design. The study was guided by research questions on how, in what way, and for whom low-cost Foundation-Assisted Schools (FASs) under PPPs policy design improve access, quality, and equity. The Realist Evaluation theoretical framework and the qualitative study design approach were employed. The data included policy documents, 25 semistructured interviews, and focus group discussions with the FAS stakeholders. This study's findings indicate that FASs under PPPs in education have some advantages over government-run schools, specifically in governance. However, the broader impact of PPP reforms in education through the low-cost schools model still does not result in increased access, quality, and equity to meet the rising demand for education in Pakistan. The implication of this study for policymakers and future researchers is to design more contextually framed model PPPs in education that work for local needs.

title: Unbundling Business Education: A Review of Micro-Credentials as Drivers of Higher Education Innovation and Labor Market Alignment
abstract: This review examines how micro-credentials are reshaping business education through modular, flexible, and skills-oriented credentialing. Drawing on recent literature published between 2015 and 2025, the article synthesizes five themes of adoption drivers, institutional and curriculum innovation, labor-market alignment, stakeholder tensions, and implementation challenges. The review finds that micro-credentials can expand access, support lifelong learning, and improve responsiveness to changing skill demands. However, their value remains constrained by uneven quality assurance, fragmented policy frameworks, uncertain employer recognition, and risks of socioeconomic exclusion. The article argues that micro-credentials should not be treated as a simple replacement for degrees, but as part of a broader credential ecosystem requiring academic coherence, transparent recognition, and equitable access. It contributes a multi-stakeholder framework for understanding how micro-credentials may support higher education reform while preserving the wider educational purposes of business schools.

title: Beyond the Screen: How Gender and Professional Experience Influence Technostress Among EFL Teachers
abstract: This study examined antecedents of technostress and evaluated the extent to which gender and teaching experience influenced technostress among Iranian private-sector EFL teachers. A mixed-methods design was employed, in which 303 teachers completed an adapted version of Tarafdar et al.’s Technostress Scale, and a purposive subsample of 25 participants participated in subsequent semi-structured interviews. The statistical analyses yielded no statistically significant differences in technostress by gender or across teaching-experience profiles. The interview findings, however, delineated privacy invasion, work overload, limited digital literacy, lack of physical interaction, work–home conflict, and emotional exhaustion as prominent stressors associated with heightened technostress.

title: Effect of the 7E Learning Cycle Model Integrated with Computer Animation on Students’ Science Process Skills
abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the effectiveness of the 7E learning cycle model integrated with computer animations on secondary school students’ Science Process Skills (SPS) in the context of biology education in Ethiopia. A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design was used. In total, 151 grade 10 students from three intact classes in the Metekel Zone, Ethiopia, were divided into three groups: Treatment Group 1 (TG1, n = 51) was taught using the 7E model along with computer animation (CA); Treatment Group 2 (TG2, n = 48) was taught using only the 7E model; and the Control Group (CG, n = 52), which involved conventional instruction. The topic “food making and growth in plants” was taught for two months. The SPST test was administered before and after the treatment to measure the integrated science process skills of students. Data analysis was done using descriptive statistics, ANOVA, and MANOVA. Pre-test analysis confirmed no significant differences in SPS among groups or between genders at baseline. title: English Teachers’ Classroom Practices for Teaching Literary Texts in the EFL Classroom
abstract: This study investigates the teaching practices of English teachers (ETs) in Nepal's secondary schools’ English as Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms, focusing on literary texts instruction. Using a quantitative research design, data were collected through observations of 14 purposively selected ETs' classes in Surkhet, Nepal, using a validated dichotomous checklist. The findings reveal that ETs promote student motivation through active engagement in their classes, however, they are unable to address the gaps in adapting diverse learning styles, resource management, collaborative activities, and formative assessment. Based on findings, the study recommends structured classroom interactions and reflective assessments for teachers. It also offers insights for school administrators to develop resource-rich classrooms and teacher training programs that enhance literature pedagogy in EFL settings.

title: Modeling Pre-service Management Teachers' Professional Knowledge and Self-efficacy in Teaching: An Implication Study for Quality Education
abstract: Teaching self-efficacy is a critical factor influencing teachers’ instructional effectiveness and professional performance. This study models the influence of professional knowledge (content knowledge, general pedagogical knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge) on teaching self-efficacy among Pre-service Management Teachers (PMTs). This study employs a quantitative approach with an explanatory research design. Data were collected from 101 PMTs using a structured questionnaire. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares - Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The results revealed that content knowledge, general pedagogical knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge significantly influences PMTs’ teaching self-efficacy. Among the predictors, pedagogical content knowledge demonstrated the strongest influence on teaching self-efficacy, followed by general pedagogical knowledge, while content knowledge showed a smaller but significant effect. The model explained a substantial proportion of variance in teaching self-efficacy (R 2 = 0.698), indicating strong predictive power. Importance–performance map analysis further showed that pedagogical content knowledge had the highe

title: Administrative Blindness in School Principals: Voices From the Field
abstract: Administrative blindness, which is an administrative disease that occurs in principals, refers to the situation where principals fail to recognize, identify, or remain insensitive to teachers’ achievements, problems, weaknesses, risks, or opportunities that may occur. This study aims to reveal the experiences of 15 middle school teachers in Izmir, 2023–2024, about administrative blindness in school principals. The study was conducted with the qualitative phenomenology design. Teachers defined administrative blindness as perceptual, managerial, and communication inadequacy. The reasons for blindness were identified as personal characteristics, training and equipment, communication problems, power and control problems, and socio-psychological problems. Administrative blindness affects schools in different ways. As a result of the research, recommendations were made, such as creating workshops, training programs, and feedback mechanisms for principals to overcome their perceptual inadequacies and to prevent blindness; conducting research to find out whether administrative blindness differs at different levels and how it is perceived by students and parents.

title: Formulation and Validation of Integrated Holistic Movement Practices Program for Adolescents from Diverse Backgrounds to Enhance Their Mental and Cognitive Well-Being
abstract: As adolescence is a crucial period of neurobiological and socioemotional development, it is vital to develop and implement interventions that promote their holistic growth and well-being. This study focused on the formulation and validation of the Integrated Holistic Movement Practices Program for Adolescents (IHMPP-A) from diverse backgrounds to augment their mental and cognitive well-being. The study proposes a theoretically coherent conceptual model to test the program's effectiveness in enhancing adolescent students’ mindfulness, mental health, and cognitive flexibility. The IHMPP-A is a school-based 12-week intervention program, comprising 12 different modules of evidence-based yoga postures, breathing exercises, and mindfulness practices. Each module is transacted weekly thrice in sessions of 60 min. The program content was validated by 14 experts using Lawshe's content validity ratio. Empirical validation showed significant gains in the experimental group in mindfulness, mental health, and cognitive flexibility.
